absent: Lock type and memory ordering of the jump label mutex and the code patching performed by jump label updates
Meaning and enforcement of the static key use check macro
Increment path, last reference predicate, and direct decrement behavior
Full layouts of static key and jump entry and their accessor semantics
Entry sorting order and architecture transform details beyond the default no operation
Module structure fields, reference counting, and notifier framework behavior
Kallsyms storage, name expansion, address helpers, sequence helpers, and value visibility policy
BPF iterator runtime, program invocation, and type registration mechanics
Proc and sequence file framework semantics and iterator reset and update helpers

findings.text: Provides query and toggle operations for static keys: a count query, paired enable operations and paired disable operations, each with a variant that assumes CPU read protection is already held and an outer variant that acquires it internally.

The enabled counter has disabled, enabled and transitional meanings. The count query reports transitional as enabled. Enable proceeds from disabled through transitional with a code update in between and then to enabled. Disable proceeds from enabled to disabled with an update. Calls already in the requested state return early.

Enable, disable, boot initialization, read-only sealing and module notification all require CPU hotplug read protection and serialize the check plus update sequence with the jump label mutex. Inner variants assert the CPU protection is held while outer variants acquire and release it around the inner call.

Provides deferred release for static keys: a direct CPU-locked decrement, a deferred decrement that only schedules delayed work when the release reaches the last reference, a flush helper for pending delayed work, an initializer that records a timeout and binds the timeout handler, and a timeout handler that recovers the enclosing deferred object and performs the release.

Text reservation is decided by interval overlap between a query range and the code range of each jump entry. The core scan walks a contiguous entry array and can skip entries flagged as init code unless the caller indicates early boot. The module scan first resolves the owning module and treats its coming state as init.

Static key type bits distinguish true polarity from linked list mode. Helpers test true polarity, set or clear linked mode, and install either a direct entry pointer or a module tracking node while preserving the masked type bits and warning on misaligned pointers. A sealed key is a linked key whose only remaining type bits are within the mask, and sealing retains only true polarity plus linked mode.

Boot initialization runs once, sorts the core jump table, rewrites default entries through an architecture hook that is a no operation on most architectures, marks whether each entry lies in init sections, groups consecutive entries by key and points each key at its first entry. A later read-only pass seals keys that reside in read-only after init memory.
Module tracking uses a singly linked node holding a next pointer, a pointer to the first jump entry for that module and key, and the owning module pointer.

Module load sorts that module entries, marks init membership, and groups by key. Keys owned by the arriving module are pointed directly at their entries. Sealed external keys are patched immediately without tracking. Other external keys gain tracking nodes, creating a core node on first link, and are patched only when current type differs from initial type. Unload removes that module node and folds a single remaining node back into a direct entry pointer with linked mode cleared.

A module state notifier handles coming and going events under CPU and jump label protection, adding on coming with rollback on allocation failure and removing on going, converting the result to notifier status. It is registered at init with priority above tracepoints.
Exposes a text reservation query that first checks the core jump table using early boot versus running state and then, when module support is present, checks module tables.
Module text ownership requires that an address first resolves to some module and then lies within that module text or init text memory type; otherwise no owner is reported.

A boot self test uses one initially true key and one initially false key, verifying enabled state and likely and unlikely branch helpers, then disabling the true key and enabling the false key and checking the inverted expectations, then restoring the original states and repeating the cycle.

Provides iteration over kernel symbols: one operation visits every core symbol by expanding names in order and invoking a caller callback with an opportunity to yield, stopping early on nonzero callback result; another resolves a name to a contiguous sequence range and visits only that range with an address callback.

Address to symbol resolution prefers core kernel addresses, then module addresses, then BPF addresses for size and offset queries. Name lookup initializes the output buffer with termination, expands core names directly, and otherwise delegates to module lookup which walks the module list under read protection, skips unformed modules, and copies the found name with bounded length.

Build identifier suffix handling has two configuration dependent behaviors: one appends a formatted identifier only when both module name and identifier are present, warning once when the identifier is missing, and the other always produces no output.

Symbol formatting resolves an adjusted address to name plus size, offset, module and build identifier under read protection, falls back to hexadecimal when unresolved, and optionally appends offset with size and module bracket with optional build identifier. Wrappers select offset display, build identifier display, and whether backtrace callers shift the address back by one.

Symbol iteration state holds a global position plus boundary positions for module, ftrace module and BPF ranges, a numeric value, a core name offset, a type character, fixed size name and module name buffers, an exported flag, and a flag controlling whether the value may be shown.

The kallsyms sequence operations advance position through a shared update helper and render one line per named symbol, hiding the value when not permitted, showing module symbols with type case derived from exported state plus module suffix and core symbols without suffix. Stop is empty.
The BPF symbol iterator context pairs an iterator metadata pointer with a symbol iterator pointer.

The BPF symbol iterator reuses the same start and advance operations but replaces show and stop so each entry and the terminal condition invoke an attached BPF program with the current iterator state. Initialization resets the iterator and caches value visibility from current credentials.

BPF iterator registration describes the sequence operations, optional finalizer, private state size, target name, rescheduling feature, one context argument mapping the iterator field to a type identifier, and a singleton type list entry used to fill that identifier at init.

The kallsyms proc file is created at init with read only permissions and standard sequence backed open, read, seek and release operations. Open allocates private iterator state, resets it to the start, and caches value visibility from the opening file credentials rather than rechecking on every display.

Unexpected counter values, sealed key misuse, missing tracking nodes, and allocation failures trigger one time or unconditional warnings. Module addition failure propagates an error and rolls back partial tracking state.

The proc file name is kallsyms with read only mode, the jump label module notifier uses priority one above tracepoints, and the kallsyms internal header and self test log prefix are defined as fixed preprocessor names.
